lessons.title: Value Types vs Reference Types
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Value Types vs Reference Types

C# divides its type system into two broad categories: value types and reference types. Understanding the distinction is fundamental to writing correct C# code and to reasoning about performance and aliasing bugs.

Value types include int, double, decimal, bool, char, struct, and enum. A variable of a value type holds its data directly. When you assign one value-type variable to another, or pass it to a method, the runtime copies the bits -- the two variables are completely independent from that point on.

Reference types include class, string, object, array, interface, and delegate. A variable of a reference type does not hold the object itself; it holds a reference to an object stored on the managed heap. Assigning a reference-type variable to another variable copies the reference, not the object, so both variables end up pointing at the same underlying object.

- Value types typically live on the stack (or inline inside the containing object) and are copied by value.
- Reference types live on the heap, are garbage collected, and are copied by reference.
- string is a reference type but behaves like a value type for comparisons because it overrides == and is immutable.
- Nullable value types (int?) wrap a value type so it can also represent "no value," using the Nullable<T> struct.

```csharp
struct Point { public int X; public int Y; }

Point p1 = new Point { X = 1, Y = 2 };
Point p2 = p1;
p2.X = 99;
Console.WriteLine(p1.X); // still 1, p2 is an independent copy
```

Knowing which category a type belongs to tells you whether mutating a copy affects the original, which is a frequent source of subtle bugs for developers coming from purely reference-based languages.

lessons.title: Declaring Variables: var, const, readonly, and Nullable Types
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Declaring Variables: var, const, readonly, and Nullable Types

C# gives you several ways to declare variables, each with different guarantees about when the value is fixed and whether it can change.

var lets the compiler infer the variable type from the initializer expression. It is still statically typed -- var name = "Alice"; makes name a string just as if you had written it explicitly -- but it reduces repetition, especially with complex generic types. var requires an initializer and cannot be used for fields.

const declares a compile-time constant. Its value must be known at compile time (a literal or an expression of other constants) and is substituted directly into the calling code wherever it is used. Because the value is baked into the IL at compile time, changing a const in a library requires every consumer to recompile to pick up the new value.

readonly declares a field whose value can only be assigned at declaration or inside a constructor, but the value itself can be computed at runtime. Unlike const, a readonly field is resolved when the consuming code runs, not when it is compiled, so it is safer to use across assembly boundaries.

Nullable value types, written int? (shorthand for Nullable<int>), let a value type also represent the absence of a value -- something ordinary value types cannot do on their own. You check HasValue and read Value, or just compare against null directly.

- Use var for readability when the type is obvious from context.
- Use const for values that truly never change.
- Use readonly for values fixed per-instance but computed at construction time.
- Use int?/T? whenever a value type needs to represent "unknown" or "missing."

```csharp
int? quantity = null;
if (!quantity.HasValue)
{
    Console.WriteLine("Quantity not yet set");
}
```

Every variable also has a default value if declared without an initializer in certain contexts (array elements, default(T)): numeric types default to 0, bool to false, and reference types to null.

interviewQuestions.question: What is boxing and unboxing in C#, and why can they hurt performance?
interviewQuestions.answer:
Boxing is the implicit conversion of a value type instance into an object (a reference type), which requires allocating a new object on the heap and copying the value into it. Unboxing is the reverse: extracting the value back out of the boxed object into a value-type variable, which requires an explicit cast and throws an InvalidCastException if the runtime type does not match exactly.

```csharp
int number = 42;
object boxed = number;        // boxing: heap allocation
int unboxed = (int)boxed;     // unboxing: cast back
Console.WriteLine(unboxed);
```

Boxing hurts performance in two ways: it allocates heap memory for every boxed value, adding garbage collection pressure, and it adds an indirection/copy step compared to working with the value directly. This becomes significant in loops or when using older, non-generic APIs such as ArrayList or Hashtable, which store everything as object and therefore box every value type added to them.

Generic collections such as List<int> avoid this entirely: because the generic type parameter is substituted with int directly, the runtime generates a specialized version of the collection that stores int values inline, with no boxing at all. This is one of the main performance reasons generics were added to C# and remains a strong argument for preferring generic collections over their non-generic predecessors.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A legacy codebase stores thousands of integers in an ArrayList inside a hot loop, and profiling shows unexpectedly high garbage collector activity.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Using ArrayList or other non-generic, object-based APIs with value types without realizing each insertion boxes the value; assuming unboxing works with any compatible numeric type rather than requiring an exact type match.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between const and readonly, and what is a subtle versioning pitfall with const across assemblies?
interviewQuestions.answer:
Both const and readonly describe values that cannot be reassigned after initialization, but they differ in when the value is fixed and how it is resolved.

const is a compile-time constant: its value must be computable at compile time from literals or other constants, and the compiler substitutes that literal value directly into every place the constant is used, in every assembly that references it. readonly is resolved at runtime: the field can be assigned a computed value, but only at its declaration or inside a constructor, and every consumer reads the field through the normal member-access mechanism rather than having the value inlined.

```csharp
public class Config
{
    public const int MaxRetries = 3;         // baked into callers at compile time
    public static readonly DateTime Started = DateTime.Now; // resolved at runtime
}
```

The versioning pitfall: if a shared library changes public const int MaxRetries = 3; to 5 in a new release, any consuming application that was compiled against the old library still has 3 baked into its own IL and will keep using 3 until it is recompiled against the new library, even if the new DLL is dropped in at runtime. A readonly (or static readonly) field does not have this problem, because consumers always read the current value at runtime from the field itself. For this reason, public constants that might ever need to change across versions of a library are usually better expressed as static readonly fields.
interviewQuestions.scenario: Your team ships a shared NuGet package with a public const configuration value, and a consuming team reports that updating the package alone did not change the observed behavior.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Using const for values that could plausibly change in a future library version; assuming recompiling the library alone is enough to update behavior in already-compiled consumers.
interviewQuestions.followUps:

lessons.title: Ternary, Null-Coalescing, and Null-Conditional Operators
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Ternary, Null-Coalescing, and Null-Conditional Operators

C# provides several compact operators designed specifically to make conditional logic and null-handling less verbose.

The ternary conditional operator ?: evaluates a boolean condition and returns one of two expressions: condition ? whenTrue : whenFalse. It is a concise alternative to a simple if/else that assigns a value, but it should be reserved for simple expressions -- nesting ternaries deeply hurts readability.

The null-coalescing operator ?? returns its left operand if it is not null, otherwise it evaluates and returns the right operand. It is the idiomatic way to supply a fallback/default value:

```csharp
string? input = null;
string value = input ?? "default";
```

The null-coalescing assignment operator ??= (C# 8+) assigns the right-hand value to the left-hand variable only if the variable is currently null. It is shorthand for x = x ?? y; and is especially handy for lazy initialization.

The null-conditional operator ?. (and its indexer form ?[ ]) short-circuits to null instead of throwing a NullReferenceException when the object being accessed is null. Combined with ??, you get a safe access plus a fallback in one expression:

```csharp
Customer? customer = GetCustomer();
int orderCount = customer?.Orders?.Count ?? 0;
```

- Use ?: for small, single-expression branching.
- Use ?? whenever you need "this value, or a fallback."
- Use ??= to initialize a field or cache only once.
- Use ?. to avoid defensive if (x != null) chains before every member access.

These operators do not replace full if statements for complex branching, but for the common "handle null gracefully" and "pick between two values" cases, they make intent obvious at a glance and reduce boilerplate significantly.

lessons.title: Concatenation and String Interpolation
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## String Concatenation and Interpolation

C# offers multiple ways to build strings out of other values, and choosing the right one affects both readability and performance.

Concatenation with the + operator joins strings (and other types, via their ToString()) end to end. It is simple for one or two pieces, but it gets hard to read once more than a couple of values are involved, and because string is immutable, each + creates a brand-new string in memory.

String interpolation, introduced with the $ prefix ($"..."), lets you embed expressions directly inside a string literal using { }. The compiler rewrites an interpolated string into an efficient formatting call behind the scenes, so it is functionally similar to concatenation but far more readable, especially with several values:

```csharp
string name = "Priya";
int orders = 4;
Console.WriteLine($"{name} has placed {orders} orders.");
```

Interpolated strings can contain arbitrary expressions, not just variable names -- method calls, arithmetic, ternaries, and even nested format specifiers (covered in the next lesson) all work inside the braces. Use double braces {{ and }} to print a literal curly brace.

- Prefer interpolation for readability when mixing text and values.
- Prefer plain concatenation only for trivial, one-off joins.
- Avoid + concatenation inside loops that run many times -- each iteration allocates a new string. Use StringBuilder instead when building a string incrementally over many iterations.
- Interpolated strings and String.Format ultimately produce the same kind of output; interpolation is just more concise and type-checked by the compiler at the call site.

Both techniques call ToString() on non-string operands implicitly, so custom types can control how they appear in interpolated or concatenated output by overriding ToString().

lessons.title: Composite Formatting, Format Specifiers, and Verbatim Strings
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Composite Formatting, Format Specifiers, and Verbatim Strings

Beyond basic interpolation, C# gives you fine control over how a value is rendered as text.

String.Format uses composite formatting: a format string with numbered placeholders ({0}, {1}, ...) that are replaced by the corresponding arguments. It predates string interpolation and is still useful when the format string itself comes from a resource file or is otherwise not a literal known at the call site.

Both String.Format and interpolated strings support format specifiers after a colon inside the braces, which control numeric and date rendering:

- C -- currency, e.g. {amount:C} on 1234.5 gives $1,234.50 (culture-dependent; en-US shown).
- N2 -- number with thousands separators and 2 decimal places, e.g. {value:N2} gives 1,234.50.
- F2 -- fixed-point with exactly 2 decimals, no thousands separator.
- D4 -- integer padded to 4 digits with leading zeros.
- X -- hexadecimal.

```csharp
double price = 999.5;
Console.WriteLine(String.Format("{0:C}", price));
Console.WriteLine($"{price:N2}");
```

Verbatim strings, prefixed with @, disable escape-sequence processing, so backslashes are literal -- ideal for file paths and regular expressions -- and they can also span multiple lines as written. To include a double quote inside a verbatim string, double it ("").

C# 11 added raw string literals, delimited by three or more double quotes ("""..."""), which handle both escaping and multi-line text cleanly, including embedding literal quotes without doubling them, and are especially convenient for JSON or multi-line templates.

```csharp
string path = @"C:\Temp\report.txt";
string raw = """{"status": "ok"}""";
```

Choosing between these tools comes down to context: interpolation for everyday readability, composite formatting when the template is data-driven, and verbatim/raw strings whenever backslashes or multi-line text would otherwise require heavy escaping.

interviewQuestions.question: What do the C, N2, F2, D, and X format specifiers do, and how would you format a decimal value as currency and as a number with two decimal places?
interviewQuestions.answer:
Format specifiers appear after a colon inside an interpolated expression or as the format argument to String.Format, and they control how a numeric (or date) value is rendered as text.

- C formats as currency using the current culture symbol and grouping, for example {amount:C} on 1234.5 in en-US produces $1,234.50.
- N2 formats as a number with thousands separators and exactly 2 decimal places, for example {value:N2} on 1234.5 produces 1,234.50.
- F2 formats as fixed-point with exactly 2 decimals but no thousands separator, for example {value:F2} on 1234.5 produces 1234.50.
- D4 (on integer types) pads with leading zeros to a minimum total width, for example {7:D4} produces 0007.
- X formats an integer as hexadecimal, for example {255:X} produces FF.

```csharp
decimal price = 1234.5m;
Console.WriteLine($"{price:C}");  // $1,234.50
Console.WriteLine($"{price:N2}"); // 1,234.50
```

These specifiers work identically whether used inside an interpolated string or passed to String.Format, since interpolation is ultimately built on the same formatting infrastructure.

interviewQuestions.question: Explain pattern matching in C# switch expressions -- type patterns, property patterns, and relational patterns -- with an example, and describe what happens if the patterns are not exhaustive.
interviewQuestions.answer:
C# switch expressions support several kinds of patterns beyond simple equality:

- Type patterns match based on an object runtime type, optionally binding it to a new variable: case Circle c => ....
- Property patterns match based on the values of one or more properties of the matched object: case { Count: 0 } => "empty".
- Relational patterns match based on comparison against a constant: case >= 90 => "A".
- These can be combined with the and, or, and not combinators for compound conditions.

```csharp
object shape = new Circle(Radius: 2);

string description = shape switch
{
    Circle { Radius: 0 } => "a point",
    Circle c when c.Radius > 10 => "a large circle",
    Circle => "a circle",
    Square or Rectangle => "a quadrilateral",
    null => "nothing",
    _ => "an unknown shape"
};
```

Because a switch expression must produce a value for every possible input, the compiler performs a best-effort exhaustiveness analysis. If it cannot prove every case is covered (for example, patterns over an open type hierarchy without a final discard), it issues a compiler warning, and if the code actually runs with a value matching no arm and there is no discard pattern, the runtime throws a SwitchExpressionException at that point. Adding a final _ => ... arm is the normal way to guarantee both compiler silence and runtime safety.

interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Omitting the final discard pattern and assuming the compiler catches every possible runtime value, when it only warns rather than guarantees exhaustiveness for non-sealed type hierarchies; overusing when guards in a way that makes the exhaustiveness analysis much harder to reason about.

lessons.contentMarkdown:
## foreach, break, and continue

foreach is the idiomatic way to iterate over every element of a collection without manually managing an index or enumerator.

```csharp
List<string> names = new() { "Ann", "Bo", "Cy" };
foreach (string name in names)
{
    Console.WriteLine(name);
}
```

Under the hood, foreach works with anything implementing IEnumerable/IEnumerable<T>: it calls GetEnumerator() and repeatedly calls MoveNext()/reads Current until the sequence is exhausted, then disposes the enumerator. This means foreach works uniformly over arrays, List<T>, dictionaries, strings (as a sequence of char), and any custom type that implements the pattern.

Two statements let you control loop flow from inside the body, and they apply equally to for, while, do-while, and foreach:

- break immediately exits the loop entirely, skipping any remaining iterations.
- continue skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps straight to the next one.

```csharp
foreach (int n in numbers)
{
    if (n < 0) continue;   // skip negative numbers
    if (n == 0) break;      // stop entirely at the first zero
    Console.WriteLine(n);
}
```

A few practical notes:

- You cannot add or remove elements from most collections while a foreach is iterating over them -- doing so throws an InvalidOperationException because the enumerator detects the collection was modified. Iterate over a copy (e.g., .ToList()) if you need to mutate while looping.
- foreach over a List<T> or array is typically just as fast as a manual for loop in modern .NET, since the compiler and JIT specialize common cases.
- For read-only iteration where you do not need an index, foreach communicates intent more clearly than for (int i = 0; ...).

Together, break and continue let you express "stop early" and "skip this one" without wrapping the rest of the loop body in a nested if.

lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Optional Parameters, Named Arguments, params Arrays, and Overloading

C# offers several features that make method calls more flexible and expressive.

Optional parameters have a default value specified in the method signature; callers may omit them entirely:

```csharp
void Log(string message, bool urgent = false)
{
    Console.WriteLine(urgent ? $"URGENT: {message}" : message);
}

Log("Build finished");          // uses default urgent = false
Log("Disk full", urgent: true); // overrides the default
```

Named arguments let a caller specify which parameter an argument maps to by name rather than by position, which is especially useful when skipping earlier optional parameters or when the call site would otherwise be ambiguous about what each positional value means.

A params array lets a method accept a variable number of trailing arguments of the same type, which the compiler packs into an array automatically:

```csharp
int Sum(params int[] numbers)
{
    int total = 0;
    foreach (int n in numbers) total += n;
    return total;
}

Sum(1, 2, 3); // equivalent to Sum(new[] { 1, 2, 3 })
```

Method overloading lets you define multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists (different number, type, or order of parameters). The compiler picks the best match at compile time based on the argument types. Overloads must differ in their parameter signature -- you cannot overload on return type alone, because a call site like Foo(5); would not give the compiler enough information to disambiguate, since the return value might be discarded entirely.

- Optional parameters reduce the need for many overloads that just supply defaults.
- Named arguments improve readability at call sites with several parameters of the same type (e.g., booleans).
- params must be the last parameter in the list, and only one is allowed per method.
- Overload resolution prefers the most specific applicable match, and ambiguous calls are a compile error, not a runtime one.

lessons.title: Declaring and Implementing Interfaces
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Declaring and Implementing Interfaces

An interface declares a contract -- a set of members a type promises to provide -- without (traditionally) supplying any implementation itself. It is declared with the interface keyword, and by convention its name starts with a capital I:

```csharp
interface IPayable
{
    decimal CalculateAmountDue();
}
```

A class implements an interface by listing it after a colon (alongside any base class) and providing concrete bodies for every member the interface declares:

```csharp
class Invoice : IPayable
{
    public decimal Subtotal { get; set; }
    public decimal CalculateAmountDue() => Subtotal * 1.1m; // with tax
}
```

Once a class implements an interface, any instance of that class can be treated as the interface type, which is the real value of interfaces: code that only needs to call CalculateAmountDue() can be written against IPayable and work with any class that implements it, without knowing or caring about the concrete type:

```csharp
IPayable bill = new Invoice { Subtotal = 100m };
Console.WriteLine(bill.CalculateAmountDue());
```

This enables loose coupling and is the foundation of patterns like dependency injection: a method can accept an ILogger, an IRepository, or an IPayable parameter, and the caller decides which concrete implementation to supply.

- Interface members are implicitly public; you do not write access modifiers on them.
- A class implementing an interface must implement every member, or itself be declared abstract.
- Interfaces can also declare properties, events, and indexers, not just methods.
- An interface can inherit from one or more other interfaces, extending the contract further.

Interfaces describe what a type can do, deliberately leaving how entirely up to each implementing class -- a separation that makes code far easier to test and extend.

lessons.title: Declaring and Initializing Arrays
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Arrays in C#

An array is a fixed-size, ordered collection of elements of the same type, stored contiguously in memory. Once you declare an array with a given length, that length cannot change — if you need a resizable collection, you want `List<T>` instead (covered in the next lesson).

C# gives you several ways to declare and initialize arrays:

- `int[] numbers = new int[5];` creates an array of 5 elements, each defaulted to `0`.
- `int[] numbers = new int[] { 1, 2, 3 };` creates and initializes an array in one step.
- `int[] numbers = [1, 2, 3];` uses the C# 12 **collection expression** syntax, which is shorter and works across arrays, `List<T>`, and other collection types.

Arrays are zero-indexed, and accessing an index outside the valid range throws an `IndexOutOfRangeException` at runtime — the compiler cannot catch this for you, so bounds checking matters in production code.

Here is a simple example:

```csharp
string[] days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"];
foreach (var day in days)
{
    Console.WriteLine(day);
}
```

Arrays also expose a `.Length` property (not `.Count`, which is reserved for collections implementing `ICollection<T>` like `List<T>`). Multi-dimensional arrays (`int[,]`) and jagged arrays (`int[][]`) are also supported for more complex grid-like data, though most everyday code only needs single-dimensional arrays. Because arrays are reference types in C#, passing one to a method passes a reference to the same underlying memory — mutating elements inside the method affects the caller's array too.

lessons.title: Working with List<T>
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Why List<T>?

`List<T>` is the workhorse collection in C# for scenarios where the number of elements isn't known up front or needs to change over time. Internally, it wraps a resizable array, automatically growing its backing storage as you add more items.

The core operations you'll use constantly:

- `Add(item)` appends an element to the end.
- `Remove(item)` removes the first occurrence of a value (returns `false` if not found).
- `RemoveAt(index)` removes the element at a specific position.
- `Contains(item)` checks whether a value exists in the list.
- `Count` reports how many elements are currently stored (unlike arrays, there is no `.Length` on `List<T>`).

```csharp
var scores = new List<int> { 10, 20, 30 };
scores.Add(40);
scores.RemoveAt(0);
Console.WriteLine(scores.Count); // 3
```

### Array vs List<T>

Choose an array when the size is fixed and known ahead of time and you want the absolute lowest memory overhead and fastest raw indexing. Choose `List<T>` when you need to add or remove elements, don't know the final size in advance, or want access to the rich set of instance methods (`Sort`, `Find`, `AddRange`, and more) that arrays don't provide directly.

Under the hood, `List<T>` is still backed by an array, so indexed access (`list[i]`) is just as fast as array indexing — the overhead only shows up when the list needs to grow its internal buffer, which happens in amortized constant time thanks to doubling the capacity on each resize.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between an array and a List<T> in C#, and when would you choose one over the other?
interviewQuestions.answer:
An array (`T[]`) has a **fixed size** set at creation time — you cannot add or remove elements, only replace existing ones or create a new array. `List<T>` is a **resizable** collection built on top of an array; it automatically grows its internal buffer as needed and exposes methods like `Add`, `Remove`, `Insert`, and `Sort`.

Key differences:

- Arrays use `.Length`; `List<T>` uses `.Count`.
- Arrays cannot grow or shrink; `List<T>` can.
- Arrays have slightly less memory overhead and no resize cost, since the size never changes.

```csharp
int[] fixedScores = [90, 85, 77];
var dynamicScores = new List<int> { 90, 85, 77 };
dynamicScores.Add(100); // fine
// fixedScores has no Add method
```

Use an array when the collection size is fixed and known in advance (e.g. RGB values, a fixed lookup table). Use `List<T>` for everything else — most application code dealing with collections of unknown or changing size should default to `List<T>`.

interviewQuestions.question: List<T>.Remove(item) has to search for the value before removing it. What is its time complexity, and how does that affect performance for large lists? What alternatives exist if removals are frequent?
interviewQuestions.answer:
`List<T>.Remove(item)` performs a **linear search** (O(n)) to find the first matching element, and then shifts all subsequent elements down by one position to fill the gap, which is also O(n). So a single `Remove` call is O(n), and removing `m` items this way is O(n * m) in the worst case.

For small lists this is negligible, but for large lists with frequent removals it becomes a bottleneck.

```csharp
var list = new List<int> { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 };
list.Remove(3); // searches, then shifts 4 and 5 left
```

If you need frequent removals (especially by key), consider:

- `HashSet<T>` or `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` for O(1) average-case lookup and removal when you don't need ordering.
- `LinkedList<T>` if you frequently remove from the middle and already hold a reference to the node (removal is O(1) once you have the node, but finding the node is still O(n)).
- Marking items as 'removed' with a flag and batch-compacting later, if removal happens inside a hot loop.

The right choice depends on whether you need ordering, how you look items up, and how often removals happen relative to reads.

lessons.title: Dictionary<TKey,TValue> Basics
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Storing Key/Value Pairs

`Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` stores data as key/value pairs and gives you near-constant-time lookup by key using a hash table internally. It's the go-to collection whenever you need to look something up by a unique identifier rather than scanning a list.

You can initialize one with an object initializer, using indexer syntax:

```csharp
var inventory = new Dictionary<string, int>
{
    ["Widgets"] = 10,
    ["Gadgets"] = 5
};
```

Adding and updating values:

- `dictionary[key] = value;` adds a new entry or **overwrites** an existing one for that key.
- `dictionary.Add(key, value);` adds a new entry but **throws `ArgumentException`** if the key already exists.
- `dictionary.TryGetValue(key, out value)` is the safe way to look up a value — it returns `true`/`false` instead of throwing, and gives you the value through the `out` parameter when found.

Direct indexer access (`dictionary[key]`) throws `KeyNotFoundException` if the key isn't present, so it should only be used when you are certain the key exists (for example, right after adding it yourself). For any lookup where the key's presence isn't guaranteed, `TryGetValue` or `ContainsKey` is the safer and more idiomatic choice, and `TryGetValue` is preferred over `ContainsKey` followed by an indexer lookup because it avoids searching the hash table twice.

lessons.title: Iterating and Avoiding KeyNotFoundException
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Iterating a Dictionary

A `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` implements `IEnumerable<KeyValuePair<TKey, TValue>>`, so you can iterate it directly with `foreach`, and each item you get back exposes `.Key` and `.Value`:

```csharp
foreach (KeyValuePair<string, int> pair in inventory)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{pair.Key}: {pair.Value}");
}
```

If you only need the keys or only the values, use the `.Keys` and `.Values` properties, which avoid allocating pairs you don't need:

- `foreach (var key in inventory.Keys)`
- `foreach (var value in inventory.Values)`

### Avoiding KeyNotFoundException

The most common runtime error with dictionaries is accessing a missing key directly through the indexer:

```csharp
int missing = inventory["Sprockets"]; // throws KeyNotFoundException if absent
```

The safe pattern is always `TryGetValue`:

```csharp
int count = inventory.TryGetValue("Sprockets", out int value) ? value : 0;
```

This single call both checks for existence and retrieves the value, avoiding a double hash lookup and the risk of an unhandled exception crashing your program. Another subtlety worth knowing: the enumeration order of a `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` is **not guaranteed** by the documented contract, even though in practice it often reflects insertion order for simple cases. Never write code that depends on a specific iteration order — if order matters, use a `SortedDictionary<TKey, TValue>` or sort the pairs explicitly before use.

lessons.title: LINQ Method Syntax: Where, Select, OrderBy, GroupBy, Aggregate
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Composing Queries with Method Syntax

LINQ method syntax chains extension methods defined on `IEnumerable<T>` (and `IQueryable<T>` for databases) to filter, transform, and summarize data declaratively, instead of writing manual loops.

The core operators you'll reach for constantly:

- `Where(predicate)` filters elements matching a condition.
- `Select(selector)` projects each element into a new shape.
- `OrderBy` / `OrderByDescending` sorts elements by a key.
- `FirstOrDefault(predicate)` returns the first match, or the type's default value (e.g. `0`, `null`) if none match.
- `GroupBy(keySelector)` groups elements that share a common key.
- `Aggregate(seed, func)` reduces a sequence to a single accumulated value.

```csharp
var topScores = scores
    .Where(s => s > 50)
    .OrderByDescending(s => s)
    .Take(3);
```

These operators are designed to be **chained**, with each one taking an `IEnumerable<T>` and returning another one, letting you build up a pipeline that reads top-to-bottom in the order operations are logically applied. `GroupBy` is particularly useful for bucketing data — for example, grouping orders by customer or words by their first letter — and returns a sequence of `IGrouping<TKey, TElement>` objects, where each group itself is enumerable and exposes a `.Key`. `Aggregate` is the general-purpose reduction operator behind more specific ones like `Sum` and `Count` — most everyday code reaches for the specific operator, but `Aggregate` is there when you need a custom accumulation, such as building a running total with custom logic or concatenating values with specific formatting.

lessons.title: Query Syntax and Deferred Execution
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Query Syntax

LINQ query syntax mirrors SQL and compiles down to the exact same method calls as method syntax:

```csharp
var result = from n in numbers
             where n % 2 == 0
             orderby n descending
             select n;
```

The compiler translates this into `numbers.Where(n => n % 2 == 0).OrderByDescending(n => n)` before producing IL, so there is no behavioral or performance difference between the two syntaxes — it's purely a readability choice, and query syntax particularly shines for joins and multi-level `from` clauses.

### Deferred Execution

Most LINQ operators don't actually run when you write them — they build up a description of the query that only executes when you **enumerate** it (with `foreach`, `ToList()`, `Count()`, and similar). This is called **deferred execution**.

```csharp
var query = numbers.Where(n => n > 2); // nothing has run yet

numbers.Add(99); // mutating the source BEFORE enumeration

foreach (var n in query) // the query runs NOW, and sees the 99
{
    Console.WriteLine(n);
}
```

Because the query re-reads the source collection at enumeration time, any changes made to that source between defining the query and enumerating it are picked up. This is a frequent source of subtle bugs: developers often assume a LINQ expression is evaluated immediately, like a snapshot, when in fact it behaves more like a recipe that's only cooked when you ask for the result. If you need a stable snapshot, call `.ToList()` or `.ToArray()` right after building the query to force immediate execution.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between deferred LINQ operators like Where and Select versus immediate ones like ToList, Count, and First? How does this distinction affect multiple-enumeration performance?
interviewQuestions.answer:
Deferred operators (`Where`, `Select`, `OrderBy`, `GroupBy`, `Skip`, `Take`, and query-syntax expressions) return an `IEnumerable<T>` that represents an unexecuted query — no work happens until you iterate it. Immediate operators (`ToList`, `ToArray`, `ToDictionary`, `Count()`, `First()`, `Sum()`, `Any()`) force the query to run right away and return a concrete result.

The performance trap is **re-enumerating a deferred query multiple times**: each enumeration re-runs the entire pipeline from the source, including any expensive filtering, projection, or even a database round-trip if the source is `IQueryable<T>` (e.g. Entity Framework).

```csharp
var expensiveQuery = data.Where(x => IsSlowCheck(x));

int count = expensiveQuery.Count();   // runs the whole pipeline once
var list = expensiveQuery.ToList();   // runs the whole pipeline AGAIN
```

If `IsSlowCheck` does real work (a web call, disk I/O, a heavy computation), this code does that work **twice**. The fix is to materialize once and reuse the result:

```csharp
var results = data.Where(x => IsSlowCheck(x)).ToList(); // materialized once
int count = results.Count;
var list = results;
```

As a rule of thumb: if you're going to use the same query result more than once, call `.ToList()` (or `.ToArray()`) immediately after building it, and work with that materialized collection from then on.

Assuming IEnumerable<T> results are cached automatically after the first enumeration, when in fact LINQ makes no such guarantee.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between LINQ method syntax and query syntax, and are they functionally equivalent?
interviewQuestions.answer:
LINQ offers two syntaxes that compile down to the same thing:

- **Method syntax** chains extension methods directly: `numbers.Where(n => n > 2).Select(n => n * 10)`.
- **Query syntax** reads more like SQL: `from n in numbers where n > 2 select n * 10`.

```csharp
// Method syntax
var a = numbers.Where(n => n > 2).OrderBy(n => n);

// Query syntax - compiles to the same method calls
var b = from n in numbers
        where n > 2
        orderby n
        select n;
```

The C# compiler translates query syntax into method syntax at compile time, so both produce identical IL and identical runtime behavior — there's no performance difference between them. Query syntax reads naturally for operations with a SQL-like structure, especially joins (`join ... on ... equals ...`) and multiple `from` clauses (for flattening nested collections), while method syntax is usually more concise and is required for operators that have no query-syntax keyword, such as `Count()`, `FirstOrDefault()`, `Sum()`, or `Aggregate()`.

In practice, many codebases mix the two: query syntax for the filtering/selection shape, then a trailing method call like `.ToList()` or `.FirstOrDefault()` that query syntax can't express on its own.

Not realizing some LINQ operators (like Count, FirstOrDefault, Sum) have no query-syntax keyword and must be tacked on as a method call even within an otherwise query-syntax expression.

interviewQuestions.question: When should you create a custom exception type instead of reusing a built-in one like ArgumentException or InvalidOperationException?
interviewQuestions.answer:
Reach for a **built-in** exception type when the failure matches its well-known semantics exactly:

- `ArgumentException` / `ArgumentNullException` / `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` for bad method arguments.
- `InvalidOperationException` for calling something in the wrong state (e.g. reading from a closed stream).
- `NotSupportedException`, `TimeoutException`, `FormatException` for their respective well-understood scenarios.

Create a **custom** exception type when:

- The failure represents a distinct **domain concept** that callers need to handle differently from other failures (e.g. `InsufficientFundsException`, `OrderValidationException`).
- You need to attach **extra structured data** to the exception beyond a message (an error code, a list of validation failures, an entity ID).
- You want callers across your codebase (or a public API/library) to be able to catch that specific domain failure without relying on message-string matching.

```csharp
public class InsufficientFundsException : Exception
{
    public decimal Shortfall { get; }
    public InsufficientFundsException(decimal shortfall)
        : base("Insufficient funds for this transaction.")
        => Shortfall = shortfall;
}
```

Avoid creating a custom exception purely to add a different message for an otherwise ordinary invalid-argument case — that's what the built-in types with a custom message argument are for. Over-creating exception types also bloats the catch-clause surface callers need to handle; keep custom types reserved for genuinely distinct, actionable failure modes.

interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Creating a new custom exception type for every single validation message instead of reusing ArgumentException with a descriptive message. Conversely, overusing InvalidOperationException for genuinely distinct domain failures that callers need to handle differently, making catch blocks ambiguous.

lessons.title: Reading and Writing Text Files with File.ReadAllText/WriteAllText
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Simple Whole-File Operations

For small to moderate text files, the `File` class's static convenience methods are the simplest way to read and write content in a single call, without manually managing a stream.

```csharp
File.WriteAllText("notes.txt", "Meeting at 10am");
string content = File.ReadAllText("notes.txt");
```

- `File.WriteAllText(path, contents)` creates the file if it doesn't exist, or **overwrites** it completely if it does.
- `File.ReadAllText(path)` reads the entire file into a single `string`.
- `File.ReadAllLines(path)` reads the file into a `string[]`, one element per line, if you want to process it line by line without manual splitting.
- `File.Exists(path)` checks whether a file exists at the given path, returning `true`/`false` without throwing.

These methods open the file, perform the read or write, and close the file automatically, all within the single call — you don't need a `using` statement because there's no stream object left open for you to manage.

Because `WriteAllText` fully overwrites existing content by default, if you want to **append** instead, use `File.AppendAllText(path, contents)`, which adds to the end of the file instead of replacing it. For anything beyond simple whole-file reads and writes — very large files, line-by-line processing, or custom encodings — you'll want the stream-based APIs covered in the next lesson.

lessons.title: Writing async Task Methods and Awaiting Them
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## The async/await Model

An `async` method is a regular method marked with the `async` modifier, which unlocks the ability to use `await` inside its body. Despite the keyword, marking a method `async` doesn't make it run on a new thread by itself — it enables the compiler to transform the method into a state machine that can pause and resume around `await` points.

An async method's return type is typically one of:

- `Task` — for an async method that doesn't return a value (the async equivalent of `void`).
- `Task<T>` — for an async method that returns a value of type `T`.
- `void` — reserved almost exclusively for event handlers, since exceptions thrown from an `async void` method can't be awaited or caught normally.

```csharp
async Task<string> GetGreetingAsync()
{
    await Task.Delay(50); // simulates asynchronous work
    return "Hello, async world";
}
```

Calling an async method returns a `Task` (or `Task<T>`) **immediately**, representing the in-progress operation — the caller then uses `await` to suspend until that operation completes, without blocking its own thread in the meantime. Modern C# also supports `async Task Main()` (or `async Task<int> Main()`) as your program's entry point, letting you `await` directly at the top level of your application instead of wrapping everything in a synchronous bootstrapping method.

lessons.title: Task.Run, Task.WhenAll, and Exception Handling in Async Code
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Offloading Work and Running Tasks Concurrently

`Task.Run` schedules a delegate to run on the thread pool, which is the right tool for **CPU-bound** work you want to move off the current thread (for example, off a UI thread so it stays responsive). It is not needed, and is actively wasteful, for naturally asynchronous I/O-bound operations (network calls, file I/O) that already have a proper async API — those should be awaited directly rather than wrapped in `Task.Run`.

```csharp
int result = await Task.Run(() => ExpensiveCalculation(1000));
```

`Task.WhenAll` lets you run several tasks **concurrently** and await their combined completion, instead of awaiting them one after another:

```csharp
var task1 = FetchUserAsync(1);
var task2 = FetchUserAsync(2);
await Task.WhenAll(task1, task2); // both run concurrently, not sequentially
```

This is significantly faster than `await task1; await task2;` when the tasks are independent, since the second one doesn't have to wait for the first to finish before starting.

### Exception Handling

Wrap `await`ed calls in ordinary `try`/`catch` blocks exactly as you would synchronous code — exceptions thrown inside an async method (or inside a task passed to `Task.WhenAll`) propagate naturally to the `await` expression. One subtlety: `Task.WhenAll` only rethrows the **first** faulted task's exception at the `await`, though the `Task` object itself exposes all of them via its `.Exception.InnerExceptions` collection if you need to inspect every failure.

lessons.title: Delegate Types: Func, Action, Predicate, and Multicast Delegates
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Functions as Values

Delegates let you treat a method like any other value — store it in a variable, pass it as a parameter, and invoke it later. Rather than declaring custom delegate types for every scenario, C# provides generic built-in ones that cover almost every case:

- `Action<T1, ...>` — a method that returns nothing.
- `Func<T1, ..., TResult>` — a method that returns `TResult` (the final type parameter).
- `Predicate<T>` — a method that takes a `T` and returns `bool`, commonly used by methods like `List<T>.Find`.

```csharp
Func<int, int> square = x => x * x;
Action<string> log = msg => Console.WriteLine($"[LOG] {msg}");
Console.WriteLine(square(5)); // 25
```

### Multicast Delegates

Delegates in C# are inherently **multicast** — a single delegate variable can reference more than one method, and invoking it calls each in the order they were added, using `+=` to subscribe and `-=` to unsubscribe:

```csharp
Action<string> notify = msg => Console.WriteLine($"Email: {msg}");
notify += msg => Console.WriteLine($"SMS: {msg}");
notify("Order shipped"); // prints both lines, in order
```

For delegates that **return a value** (like `Func<T>`), invoking a multicast delegate still calls every subscriber, but only the return value of the **last** one invoked is actually returned to the caller — the intermediate results are discarded. This is an important gotcha: multicast delegates are best suited to `Action`-style, fire-and-forget notification scenarios (which is exactly what events are built on) rather than chaining multiple value-returning computations.

interviewQuestions.question: What are generic type constraints like where T : class, new(), and why would you add them to a generic class or method?
interviewQuestions.answer:
A constraint restricts what types can be substituted for a type parameter `T`, which lets the compiler allow operations on `T` that wouldn't otherwise be safe for an arbitrary unknown type. Without any constraint, the compiler only lets you treat `T` as `object` — you can't call `.CompareTo()`, construct a `new T()`, or assume it's a reference type, because some arbitrary `T` might not support that.

Common constraints:

- `where T : class` — `T` must be a reference type (allows comparing to `null` with `==`, among other things).
- `where T : struct` — `T` must be a non-nullable value type.
- `where T : new()` — `T` must have an accessible parameterless constructor, enabling `new T()` inside the generic code.
- `where T : IComparable<T>` — `T` must implement a given interface, enabling calls like `a.CompareTo(b)`.
- `where T : BaseClass` — `T` must be `BaseClass` or a type derived from it.

```csharp
public class Repository<T> where T : class, new()
{
    public T CreateNew() => new T(); // only legal because of the new() constraint
}
```

Constraints are also frequently combined, and multiple constraints are separated by commas, with any base-class constraint listed first, interface constraints next, and `new()` always last if present. Constraints make generic code both safer (the compiler enforces the capability requirement at every call site) and more capable (you can call members that only the constraint guarantees exist).

interviewQuestions.question: How do generics avoid boxing and unboxing for value types compared to object-based collections like ArrayList, and why does this matter for performance?
interviewQuestions.answer:
Before generics existed (pre-C# 2.0), non-generic collections like `ArrayList` stored everything as `object`. Storing a value type (like `int`) into an `object`-typed slot requires **boxing** — allocating a new object on the heap to wrap the value — and reading it back out requires **unboxing**, casting it back to the value type. Every single element access pays this allocation/copy cost.

```csharp
ArrayList list = new ArrayList();
list.Add(42);           // boxing: allocates a heap object to hold 42
int x = (int)list[0];   // unboxing: copies the value back out, with a runtime type check
```

With generics, `List<int>` is compiled (via the CLR's generic specialization for value types) to store `int` values **directly**, with no boxing at all:

```csharp
List<int> list = new List<int>();
list.Add(42); // stored directly as an int, no heap allocation per element
int x = list[0]; // direct read, no cast or unboxing
```

The performance impact compounds with scale: a loop boxing a million integers performs a million extra heap allocations, bloating memory usage and generating significant garbage-collection pressure, whereas the generic version allocates once for the backing array and stores the raw values inline. This is one of the core reasons the generic collections (`List<T>`, `Dictionary<TKey,TValue>`, `Queue<T>`, `Stack<T>`) in `System.Collections.Generic` replaced the older `System.Collections` non-generic types almost entirely in modern C# code, beyond just the added compile-time type safety generics also provide (catching type mismatches at compile time instead of a runtime `InvalidCastException`).
